claim: Islet amyloidosis by IAPP contributes to pancreatic β-cell death in diabetes.
source: Islet amyloidosis by IAPP contributes to pancreatic β-cell death in diabetes, but the nature of toxic IAPP species remains elusive.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known fact in the field, supported by the broader literature context.

claim: The nature of toxic IAPP species remains elusive.
source: Islet amyloidosis by IAPP contributes to pancreatic β-cell death in diabetes, but the nature of toxic IAPP species remains elusive.
evidence: This statement reflects the gap in knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: Toxic IAPP species are globally flexible, low order oligomers.
source: These globally flexible, low order oligomers upregulate pro-inflammatory markers and induce reactive oxygen species.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data including photochemical cross-linking, CD, and 2D IR.

claim: Toxic IAPP oligomers upregulate pro-inflammatory markers.
source: These globally flexible, low order oligomers upregulate pro-inflammatory markers and induce reactive oxygen species.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data showing upregulation of Ccl2 and Il1b in Figure 3A and B.

claim: Toxic IAPP oligomers induce reactive oxygen species.
source: These globally flexible, low order oligomers upregulate pro-inflammatory markers and induce reactive oxygen species.
evidence: This is supported by DHE fluorescence assays and NOX1 upregulation shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: Toxic IAPP oligomers do not bind 1-anilnonaphthalene-8-sulphonic acid (ANS).
source: They do not bind 1-anilnonaphthalene-8-sulphonic acid and lack extensive β-sheet structure.
evidence: This is demonstrated by ANS fluorescence experiments shown in Figure 7B and C.

claim: Toxic IAPP oligomers lack extensive β-sheet structure.
source: They do not bind 1-anilnonaphthalene-8-sulphonic acid and lack extensive β-sheet structure.
evidence: This is supported by 2D IR spectroscopy data in Figure 6, showing less than 15% β-sheet content.

claim: Aromatic interactions modulate but are not required for IAPP toxicity.
source: Aromatic interactions modulate, but are not required for toxicity.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments with 3xL-IAPP mutant (Figure 9), which lacks aromatic residues but is still toxic, though less so than h-IAPP.

claim: Not all IAPP oligomers are toxic.
source: Not all IAPP oligomers are toxic; toxicity depends on their partially structured conformational states.
evidence: This is supported by data showing that r-IAPP, I26P-IAPP, and TM-IAPP form oligomers but are not toxic (Figure 5).

claim: IAPP toxicity depends on the partially structured conformational states of oligomers.
source: Not all IAPP oligomers are toxic; toxicity depends on their partially structured conformational states.
evidence: This is inferred from CD and 2D IR data comparing toxic h-IAPP oligomers with non-toxic variants.

claim: Some anti-amyloid agents paradoxically prolong cytotoxicity by prolonging the lifetime of toxic species.
source: Some anti-amyloid agents paradoxically prolong cytotoxicity by prolonging the lifetime of the toxic species.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments with I26P-IAPP as an inhibitor (Figure 10), showing extended lag phase and prolonged toxicity.

claim: Toxic h-IAPP species are transient, pre-amyloid lag phase intermediates.
source: Toxic h-IAPP species are transient, pre-amyloid lag phase intermediates that upregulate oxidative stress, inflammation and apoptosis
evidence: This is shown by time-resolved toxicity assays (Figure 2B) correlated with thioflavin-T binding and TEM (Figure 2C).

claim: h-IAPP toxicity to β-cells is time-dependent.
source: h-IAPP toxicity to β-cells is observed to be time-dependent; amyloid fibrils are not toxic, but species populated in the lag phase are.
evidence: This is demonstrated by Alamar Blue reduction assays at different time points (Figure 2B).

claim: h-IAPP amyloid fibrils are not toxic to β-cells.
source: h-IAPP toxicity to β-cells is observed to be time-dependent; amyloid fibrils are not toxic, but species populated in the lag phase are.
evidence: This is shown by cell viability assays with saturation phase samples (Figure 2B).

claim: h-IAPP lag phase intermediates are toxic to pancreatic islets.
source: The data provide direct evidence that the lag phase intermediates are toxic to cells in tissue.
evidence: This is demonstrated by ex vivo islet viability assays (Figure 2F).

claim: h-IAPP lag phase intermediates upregulate Ccl2 mRNA expression.
source: h-IAPP lag phase intermediates also induce an increase in Ccl2 and Il1b mRNA expression
evidence: This is shown by qPCR data in Figure 3A.

claim: h-IAPP lag phase intermediates upregulate Il1b mRNA expression.
source: h-IAPP lag phase intermediates also induce an increase in Ccl2 and Il1b mRNA expression
evidence: This is shown by qPCR data in Figure 3B.

claim: h-IAPP lag phase intermediates increase ROS production.
source: h-IAPP lag phase intermediates also induce an increase in Ccl2 and Il1b mRNA expression, an increase in ROS production
evidence: This is demonstrated by DHE fluorescence assays (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).

claim: h-IAPP lag phase intermediates upregulate NADPH oxidase 1 (NOX1) protein expression.
source: h-IAPP lag phase intermediates also induce an increase in Ccl2 and Il1b mRNA expression, an increase in ROS production, upregulation of NADPH oxidase 1 (NOX1) protein expression
evidence: This is shown by Western blot data in Figure 3D.

claim: h-IAPP lag phase intermediates increase cleaved caspase-3 production.
source: h-IAPP lag phase intermediates also induce an increase in Ccl2 and Il1b mRNA expression, an increase in ROS production, upregulation of NADPH oxidase 1 (NOX1) protein expression, and an increase in cleaved caspase-3 production
evidence: This is demonstrated by cleaved caspase-3 colorimetric assays (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).

claim: h-IAPP toxic species are soluble.
source: Ultracentrifugation studies demonstrate that h-IAPP toxic species are soluble.
evidence: This is shown by ultracentrifugation experiments where 94% of lag phase peptide remains in the supernatant (Figure 4).

claim: At least 88% of h-IAPP fibrils are pelleted at 20,000 g for 20 min.
source: At least 88% of h-IAPP is pelleted in the sample of fibrils, even at these low g-forces
evidence: This is stated based on ultracentrifugation experiments.

claim: 94% of h-IAPP lag phase intermediates remain in the supernatant after ultracentrifugation at 20,000 g for 20 min.
source: while 94% of the peptide in the sample of toxic lag phase intermediates remains in the supernatant.
evidence: This is stated based on ultracentrifugation experiments.

claim: The ensemble of h-IAPP lag phase intermediates exhibits partial apparent helical structure.
source: Characterization of the ensemble of h-IAPP lag phase intermediates by circular dichroism (CD) reveals partial apparent helical structure.
evidence: This is shown by CD spectra in Figure 4F showing minima at 208 nm and 220 nm.

claim: Toxic h-IAPP lag phase intermediates contain a distribution of oligomers ranging from monomers to hexamers.
source: The data reveal a distribution of oligomers ranging from monomers to hexamers at time points of toxicity
evidence: This is demonstrated by photochemical cross-linking and SDS-PAGE analysis (Figure 4G and H).

claim: Dimers, trimers and tetramers are the most populated h-IAPP toxic species.
source: Analysis of apparent relative populations of h-IAPP toxic species, deduced from the gel, indicate that dimers, trimers and tetramers are the most populated species.
evidence: This is inferred from quantitative analysis of photochemical cross-linking gels (Figure 4H).

claim: A distribution of h-IAPP oligomers ranging from monomers to hexamers is populated within 10 minutes of initiating amyloid formation.
source: The dead time of the measurement (the time before the first measurement) is on the order of 10 min; a distribution of oligomers ranging from monomers to hexamers is populated within that time frame
evidence: This is shown by photochemical cross-linking experiments at early time points (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).

claim: r-IAPP is non-toxic and non-amyloidogenic in vivo.
source: r-IAPP is non-toxic and non-amyloidogenic in vivo and is widely used as a negative control in biological and biophysical/biochemical studies of h-IAPP (Westermark et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation to Westermark et al., 2011.

claim: r-IAPP is not toxic to INS-1 β-cells even at concentrations up to 84 µM and incubation times up to 96 hours.
source: To further validate the use of r-IAPP as a negative control, we carried out dose-response experiments to test the effect of incubating INS-1 β-cells with up to 6-fold higher concentrations (84 µM) of r-IAPP for up to 19-fold longer incubation times on cells (96 h) than used in the assays employed herein to assess h-IAPP toxicity. No detectable toxicity was observed for r-IAPP, even at these significantly higher concentrations (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by dose-response experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: r-IAPP forms oligomers with a distribution similar to h-IAPP.
source: Cross-linking studies (Figure 5B) reveal a broadly similar distribution of oligomers produced in solution by r-IAPP and h-IAPP, with detected species ranging from monomers to hexamers.
evidence: This is shown by photochemical cross-linking experiments (Figure 5B and C).

claim: r-IAPP oligomers appear less structured than h-IAPP oligomers.
source: CD studies reveal that r-IAPP oligomers appear less structured than their h-IAPP counterparts, as indicated by a positive signal below 190 nm and less intense signal between 218 to 222 nm (Figure 5H) in the spectrum of lag phase oligomers.
evidence: This is shown by CD spectroscopy data in Figure 5H.

claim: I26P-IAPP does not form amyloid under the conditions of the study.
source: We have previously shown that I26P-IAPP inhibits amyloid formation by h-IAPP and does not form amyloid by itself under the conditions of our studies (Abedini et al., 2007; Meng et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated based on previous publications (Abedini et al., 2007; Meng et al., 2010) and confirmed by thioflavin-T and TEM in Figure 5D and I.

claim: I26P-IAPP forms low order oligomers similar to h-IAPP.
source: Like r-IAPP, this mutant forms low order oligomers with an apparent size distribution that is similar to h-IAPP oligomers, as judged by photochemical induced cross-linking studies
evidence: This is shown by photochemical cross-linking data in Figure 5B and C.

claim: I26P-IAPP is not toxic at any time point over 35+ hours.
source: Cell viability assays carried out in parallel with biophysical studies show that I26P-IAPP is not toxic at any time point in our studies (Figure 5F and J).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Alamar Blue reduction assays in Figure 5F and J.

claim: The upper limit for β-sheet content in the ensemble of h-IAPP lag phase intermediates is on the order of 15%.
source: Based on the relative areas in Figure 6C, the upper limit for the β-sheet content in the ensemble of lag phase intermediates populated under these conditions is estimated to be on the order of 15%.
evidence: This is estimated from 2D IR spectroscopy data shown in Figure 6.

claim: h-IAPP lag phase intermediates do not bind ANS.
source: No ANS binding is observed in the lag phase, but is observed during the growth phase of amyloid formation and in the saturation phase containing fibrils (Figure 7B and C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ANS fluorescence experiments in Figure 7B and C.

claim: h-IAPP lag phase intermediates do not bind bis-ANS.
source: We also tested the ability of h-IAPP toxic intermediates to bind bis-ANS. No binding to lag phase species is observed, but the dye, like ANS, binds to h-IAPP amyloid fibrils (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown by bis-ANS fluorescence experiments in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: h-IAPP lag phase intermediates do not bind Nile Red.
source: We independently confirmed that it does not bind to the lag phase species populated in our experiments (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Nile Red fluorescence experiments in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: h-IAPP monomers and lag phase intermediates are rapidly digested by Proteinase K.
source: h-IAPP monomers and lag phase intermediates are rapidly digested by the protease, while h-IAPP amyloid fibrils are not, even after 40 min of incubation (Figure 7—figure supplement 2–14).
evidence: This is shown by MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry after Proteinase K treatment (Figure 7—figure supplements 2–14).

claim: h-IAPP amyloid fibrils are not digested by Proteinase K even after 40 min of incubation.
source: h-IAPP monomers and lag phase intermediates are rapidly digested by the protease, while h-IAPP amyloid fibrils are not, even after 40 min of incubation (Figure 7—figure supplement 2–14).
evidence: This is shown by MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry after Proteinase K treatment (Figure 7—figure supplements 2–14).

claim: Phe-15, Phe-23 and Tyr-37 are largely solvent exposed in h-IAPP lag phase intermediates.
source: The data indicate that Phe-15, Phe-23 and Tyr-37 are largely solvent exposed in the lag phase
evidence: This is demonstrated by p-cyanoPhe fluorescence experiments shown in Figure 8E.

claim: 3xL-IAPP forms amyloid more slowly than h-IAPP.
source: Thioflavin-T assays and TEM measurements confirm that the triple mutant does form amyloid more slowly than the human peptide (Figure 9B–D).
evidence: This is shown by thioflavin-T kinetics and TEM in Figure 9B–D.

claim: 3xL-IAPP exhibits time dependent toxicity with lag phase species being toxic and fibrils being non-toxic.
source: Cell viability studies show, that like h-IAPP, 3XL-IAPP exhibits time dependent toxicity; the amyloid fibrils produced by 3xL-IAPP are not toxic to β-cells, but species populated in the lag phase are
evidence: This is demonstrated by time-resolved Alamar Blue reduction assays in Figure 9E.

claim: 3xL-IAPP evokes significantly lower levels of toxicity than h-IAPP.
source: Dose-response studies show that 3xL-IAPP evokes significantly lower levels of toxicity than h-IAPP. At their respective time points of maximum toxicity, 40 μM 3xL-IAPP reduced β-cell viability to 67%, while 20 μM h-IAPP reduced β-cell viability to 35% (Figure 9F).
evidence: This is shown by dose-response experiments in Figure 9F.

claim: 3xL-IAPP is toxic despite lacking aromatic residues.
source: However, 3xL-IAPP is clearly still toxic, indicating that aromatic residues, and hence π-π interactions, are not an absolute requirement for h-IAPP toxicity, but do contribute to it.
evidence: This is demonstrated by toxicity assays with 3xL-IAPP shown in Figure 9E and F.

claim: A 1:1 addition of I26P-IAPP lengthens both the lag phase and the growth phase of h-IAPP amyloid formation.
source: Time-resolved kinetic studies of cytotoxicity and amyloid formation show that a 1:1 addition of I26P-IAPP lengthens both the lag phase and the growth phase
evidence: This is shown by thioflavin-T kinetics in Figure 10B.

claim: A 1:1 addition of I26P-IAPP increases the duration of h-IAPP toxicity proportionally to the increase in lag phase length.
source: Time-resolved kinetic studies of cytotoxicity and amyloid formation show that a 1:1 addition of I26P-IAPP lengthens both the lag phase and the growth phase, and increases the duration of toxicity proportionally (Figure 10).
evidence: This is demonstrated by concurrent toxicity and thioflavin-T assays in Figure 10A and B.

claim: The T50 value for h-IAPP amyloid formation is increased by a factor of two with 1:1 I26P-IAPP addition.
source: The value of T50 (the time required to reach 50% of the total signal change in a thioflavin-T experiment) is increased by a factor of two
evidence: This is inferred from the thioflavin-T kinetics data in Figure 10B.

claim: The lag phase length for h-IAPP amyloid formation is increased by a factor of two with 1:1 I26P-IAPP addition.
source: as is the length of the lag phase, defined here as the time required to reach 10% of the total change in thioflavin-T signal.
evidence: This is inferred from the thioflavin-T kinetics data in Figure 10B.

claim: Pancreatic islet amyloidosis by h-IAPP contributes to β-cell death in type 2 diabetes.
source: Pancreatic islet amyloidosis by the neuropancreatic hormone, human islet amyloid polypeptide (h-IAPP, also known as amylin) contributes to β-cell death, progression of T2D, islet transplant failure, as well as cardiovascular complications (Figure 1) (Potter et al., 2010; Ashcroft and Rorsman, 2012; Westermark et al., 2008; Despa et al., 2012; Abedini and Schmidt, 2013; Cao et al., 2013a).
evidence: This is stated with multiple citations supporting the claim.

claim: Pancreatic islet amyloidosis by h-IAPP contributes to progression of type 2 diabetes.
source: Pancreatic islet amyloidosis by the neuropancreatic hormone, human islet amyloid polypeptide (h-IAPP, also known as amylin) contributes to β-cell death, progression of T2D, islet transplant failure, as well as cardiovascular complications (Figure 1) (Potter et al., 2010; Ashcroft and Rorsman, 2012; Westermark et al., 2008; Despa et al., 2012; Abedini and Schmidt, 2013; Cao et al., 2013a).
evidence: This is stated with multiple citations supporting the claim.

claim: Pancreatic islet amyloidosis by h-IAPP contributes to islet transplant failure.
source: Pancreatic islet amyloidosis by the neuropancreatic hormone, human islet amyloid polypeptide (h-IAPP, also known as amylin) contributes to β-cell death, progression of T2D, islet transplant failure, as well as cardiovascular complications (Figure 1) (Potter et al., 2010; Ashcroft and Rorsman, 2012; Westermark et al., 2008; Despa et al., 2012; Abedini and Schmidt, 2013; Cao et al., 2013a).
evidence: This is stated with multiple citations supporting the claim.

claim: Pancreatic islet amyloidosis by h-IAPP contributes to cardiovascular complications.
source: Pancreatic islet amyloidosis by the neuropancreatic hormone, human islet amyloid polypeptide (h-IAPP, also known as amylin) contributes to β-cell death, progression of T2D, islet transplant failure, as well as cardiovascular complications (Figure 1) (Potter et al., 2010; Ashcroft and Rorsman, 2012; Westermark et al., 2008; Despa et al., 2012; Abedini and Schmidt, 2013; Cao et al., 2013a).
evidence: This is stated with multiple citations supporting the claim.

claim: Mature h-IAPP is co-stored with insulin in β-cell insulin secretory granules at ~500 μM to low mM concentration range.
source: Mature, post-translationally modified h-IAPP (Figure 1A) is co-stored with insulin in the β-cell insulin secretory granules (~500 μM to low mM concentration range)
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about h-IAPP biology.

claim: h-IAPP is co-secreted with insulin into the extracellular space within pancreatic islets.
source: and is co-secreted with insulin into the extracellular space within the pancreatic islets, where it then diffuses into blood vessels and enters the circulation (pM concentrations).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about h-IAPP biology.

claim: h-IAPP plays an adaptive role in metabolism and glucose homeostasis.
source: The polypeptide plays an adaptive role in metabolism and glucose homeostasis
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about h-IAPP function.

claim: Both extracellular and intracellular h-IAPP oligomers contribute to islet β-cell toxicity.
source: Existing data indicate that both extracellular and intracellular h-IAPP oligomers contribute to islet β-cell toxicity.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of existing literature.

claim: Amyloid deposits associated with type 2 diabetes are extracellular.
source: Histological studies show that amyloid deposits associated with T2D are extracellular (Westermark et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Westermark et al., 2011.

claim: Rodent IAPP is not toxic.
source: Rodent IAPP is not toxic and does not form amyloid (Westermark et al., 2011)
evidence: This is stated with citation to Westermark et al., 2011.

claim: Rodent IAPP does not form amyloid.
source: Rodent IAPP is not toxic and does not form amyloid (Westermark et al., 2011)
evidence: This is stated with citation to Westermark et al., 2011.

claim: There is strong evidence that extracellular oligomers induce cytotoxicity in vivo.
source: There is strong evidence that extracellular oligomers induce cytotoxicity in vivo (Westermark et al., 2011; Park et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2003; Aston-Mourney et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated with multiple citations supporting the claim.

claim: h-IAPP secretion is required for amyloid formation and β-cell toxicity in transgenic islet models expressing human-relevant levels of h-IAPP.
source: Studies using a transgenic islet model that expresses human-relevant levels of h-IAPP demonstrate that h-IAPP secretion is required for amyloid formation and β-cell toxicity (Aston-Mourney et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Aston-Mourney et al., 2011.

claim: h-IAPP oligomers activate the inflammasome.
source: as do studies showing that h-IAPP oligomers activate the inflammasome (Johnson et al., 2012; Masters et al., 2010; Park et al., 2012)
evidence: This is stated with citations to Johnson et al., 2012; Masters et al., 2010; Park et al., 2012.

claim: Extracellular h-IAPP oligomers can be transported into β-cells.
source: and recent findings that extracellular h-IAPP oligomers can be transported into β-cells (Trikha and Jeremic, 2013; Sheedy et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Trikha and Jeremic, 2013; Sheedy et al., 2013.

claim: Toxic h-IAPP oligomers can induce β-cell toxicity by both extra- and intracellular mechanisms.
source: Thus, toxic h-IAPP oligomers can induce β-cell toxicity by both extra- and intracellular mechanisms.
evidence: This is inferred from the discussion of extracellular and intracellular mechanisms.

claim: Amyloid formation by h-IAPP comprises three distinct phenomenological phases: a lag, growth and saturation phase.
source: Amyloid formation by h-IAPP, like that of other amyloidogenic proteins, comprises three distinct phenomenological phases: a lag, growth and saturation phase (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about amyloid formation kinetics.

claim: Little or no amyloid is formed in the lag phase of h-IAPP amyloid formation.
source: Little or no amyloid is formed in the lag phase and little is known about the nature of the species that populate this phase.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the lag phase.

claim: The 30% dilution of h-IAPP peptide stock solutions into cell culture does not significantly alter the distribution of oligomers.
source: Control experiments using photochemical induced cross-linking and thioflavin-T kinetic assays of amyloid formation in buffer at 25°C reveal that this modest dilution does not significantly alter the distribution of oligomers
evidence: This is demonstrated by control experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 2.

claim: The 30% dilution of h-IAPP peptide stock solutions into cell culture does not significantly alter the time course of amyloid formation.
source: nor does it significantly alter the time course of amyloid formation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by control experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 2.

claim: Dilution of h-IAPP into cell culture medium at 37°C has no significant effect on the time course of amyloid formation.
source: The same dilution into cell culture medium at 37°C has no significant effect on the time course (Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by control experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Cellular stress and inflammation have been implicated in h-IAPP induced β-cell toxicity in vitro, in mouse models and in human T2D.
source: Cellular stress and inflammation have been implicated in h-IAPP induced β-cell toxicity in vitro, in mouse models of metabolic disease and in human T2D (Westermark et al., 2011; Masters et al., 2010; Zraika et al., 2009; Janciauskiene and Ahrén, 2000; Konarkowska et al., 2005; Sakuraba et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated with multiple citations supporting the claim.

claim: No significant upregulation of cytokines is induced by h-IAPP time-zero species.
source: No significant upregulation of cytokines, ROS or cleaved caspase-3 production is induced by time-zero species or by h-IAPP amyloid fibrils
evidence: This is shown by qPCR and other assays in Figure 3.

claim: No significant upregulation of cytokines is induced by h-IAPP amyloid fibrils.
source: No significant upregulation of cytokines, ROS or cleaved caspase-3 production is induced by time-zero species or by h-IAPP amyloid fibrils
evidence: This is shown by qPCR and other assays in Figure 3.

claim: No ROS production is induced by h-IAPP time-zero species.
source: No significant upregulation of cytokines, ROS or cleaved caspase-3 production is induced by time-zero species or by h-IAPP amyloid fibrils
evidence: This is shown by DHE assays in Figure 3.

claim: No ROS production is induced by h-IAPP amyloid fibrils.
source: No significant upregulation of cytokines, ROS or cleaved caspase-3 production is induced by time-zero species or by h-IAPP amyloid fibrils
evidence: This is shown by DHE assays in Figure 3.

claim: No cleaved caspase-3 production is induced by h-IAPP time-zero species.
source: No significant upregulation of cytokines, ROS or cleaved caspase-3 production is induced by time-zero species or by h-IAPP amyloid fibrils
evidence: This is shown by caspase-3 assays in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: No cleaved caspase-3 production is induced by h-IAPP amyloid fibrils.
source: No significant upregulation of cytokines, ROS or cleaved caspase-3 production is induced by time-zero species or by h-IAPP amyloid fibrils
evidence: This is shown by caspase-3 assays in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: No toxicity or cytokine production is observed when r-IAPP is added to cultured β-cells at any time point.
source: No toxicity or cytokine production is observed when non-amyloidogenic r-IAPP is added to cultured β-cells at any time point, consistent with previous reports (Westermark et al., 2011).
evidence: This is demonstrated by toxicity and qPCR assays with r-IAPP shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: The CD spectrum of h-IAPP changes with time and eventually converts into a spectrum indicative of β-structure.
source: With further incubation, the CD spectrum of h-IAPP changes and eventually converts into a spectrum indicative of β-structure (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown by time-resolved CD spectroscopy in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The overall conformation of the ensemble of h-IAPP oligomeric intermediates in solution remains the same after ultracentrifugation.
source: The spectra are superimposable, confirming that the observed CD signal reflects the peptide in the soluble fraction and demonstrates that the overall conformation of the ensemble of oligomeric intermediates in solution remains the same after ultracentrifugation.
evidence: This is shown by comparing CD spectra before and after ultracentrifugation in Figure 4F.

claim: The distribution of h-IAPP oligomers is populated within 10 minutes and persists through the lag phase.
source: The data are consistent with independent ion mobility mass spectroscopy studies that report that a distribution of h-IAPP monomers to hexamers form within 2 min of initiating amyloid formation, and that the distribution is present later in the lag phase (Young et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Young et al., 2014 and supported by the authors' own cross-linking data.

claim: The lag phase of h-IAPP amyloid formation could be controlled by a significant structural rearrangement within an oligomeric nucleus that involves crossing a high free energy barrier.
source: The rapid formation of oligomers and their persistence through the lag phase is consistent with recently proposed models of h-IAPP amyloid formation that posit that the lag phase could be controlled by a significant structural rearrangement within an oligomeric nucleus that involves crossing a high free energy barrier (Buchanan et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as consistent with models proposed by Buchanan et al., 2013.

claim: The distribution of cross-linked h-IAPP species is significantly different from that expected for a monomeric protein.
source: Quantitative analysis of the silver stained gels reveal that the distribution of cross-linked h-IAPP species is significantly different from that expected for a monomeric protein (Figure 4H and Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparison with HP35* control protein in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: IAPP is expressed by all mammals examined to date.
source: IAPP is expressed by all mammals examined to date; the amino acid sequences are ~80% conserved between species
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation context.

claim: IAPP amino acid sequences are ~80% conserved between mammalian species.
source: IAPP is expressed by all mammals examined to date; the amino acid sequences are ~80% conserved between species
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: Not all IAPP sequences are toxic or form amyloid in vivo.
source: however not all IAPP sequences are toxic or form amyloid in vivo (Figure 5—figure supplement 1) (Betsholtz et al., 1989; Cao et al., 2013b; Westermark et al., 1990).
evidence: This is stated with citations and shown in sequence alignment in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The r-IAPP sequence differs from the h-IAPP sequence at six positions.
source: The r-IAPP sequence differs from the h-IAPP sequence at six positions and contains three Pro residues and a His-18 to Arg replacement (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is shown in the sequence alignment in Figure 5A.

claim: r-IAPP contains three Pro residues.
source: The r-IAPP sequence differs from the h-IAPP sequence at six positions and contains three Pro residues and a His-18 to Arg replacement (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is shown in the sequence alignment in Figure 5A.

claim: r-IAPP has a His-18 to Arg replacement compared to h-IAPP.
source: The r-IAPP sequence differs from the h-IAPP sequence at six positions and contains three Pro residues and a His-18 to Arg replacement (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is shown in the sequence alignment in Figure 5A.

claim: r-IAPP is not toxic over a 28 day time course.
source: Additional studies show that r-IAPP is not toxic over a 28 day time course (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated based on additional unpublished experiments.

claim: The CD spectrum of r-IAPP does not change with time.
source: In contrast to h-IAPP, the CD spectrum of non-amyloidogenic r-IAPP does not change with time and is independent of concentration over the range tested (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is shown by time-resolved CD spectroscopy in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: The CD spectrum of r-IAPP is independent of concentration over the range tested.
source: In contrast to h-IAPP, the CD spectrum of non-amyloidogenic r-IAPP does not change with time and is independent of concentration over the range tested (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is shown by concentration-dependent CD spectroscopy in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: I26P-IAPP is similar to h-IAPP in hydrophobicity.
source: I26P-IAPP is similar to h-IAPP in hydrophobicity and has an identical net charge.
evidence: This is stated and supported by hydrophobicity plots in Figure 5—figure supplement 6.

claim: I26P-IAPP has an identical net charge to h-IAPP.
source: I26P-IAPP is similar to h-IAPP in hydrophobicity and has an identical net charge.
evidence: This is stated based on the sequences.

claim: I26P-IAPP is non-amyloidogenic over 35+ hours under the study conditions.
source: but is non-amyloidogenic under these conditions over the 35+ h duration of these studies, as judged by thioflavin-T binding assays and TEM (Figure 5D and I).
evidence: This is demonstrated by thioflavin-T and TEM data in Figure 5D and I.

claim: The CD spectrum of I26P-IAPP is similar to that of r-IAPP.
source: The CD spectrum of I26P-IAPP is similar to that of r-IAPP (Figure 5H and Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is shown by CD spectroscopy in Figure 5H and Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claim: The H18R, G24P, I26P triple mutant of h-IAPP (TM-IAPP) is non-amyloidogenic.
source: The H18R, G24P, I26P triple mutant of h-IAPP (TM-IAPP) has been shown to be non-amyloidogenic and non-toxic (Wang et al., 2014b).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Wang et al., 2014b.

claim: TM-IAPP is non-toxic.
source: The H18R, G24P, I26P triple mutant of h-IAPP (TM-IAPP) has been shown to be non-amyloidogenic and non-toxic (Wang et al., 2014b).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Wang et al., 2014b.

claim: TM-IAPP oligomerizes.
source: Photochemical induced cross-linking and CD studies show that this variant also oligomerizes, even though it remains as random coil as judged by CD (Figure 5—figure supplement 5B–D).
evidence: This is shown by photochemical cross-linking in Figure 5—figure supplement 5B and C.

claim: TM-IAPP remains as random coil as judged by CD.
source: Photochemical induced cross-linking and CD studies show that this variant also oligomerizes, even though it remains as random coil as judged by CD (Figure 5—figure supplement 5B–D).
evidence: This is shown by CD spectroscopy in Figure 5—figure supplement 5D.

claim: All three non-toxic IAPP variants (r-IAPP, I26P-IAPP, TM-IAPP) have similar hydrophobicity to h-IAPP.
source: Thus, all three of the different non-toxic variants, which have similar hydrophobicity to h-IAPP, oligomerize (Figure 5—figure supplements 6 and 7).
evidence: This is shown by hydrophobicity analysis in Figure 5—figure supplements 6 and 7.

claim: Properties of polypeptides beyond their ability to oligomerize are important determinants of cellular toxicity.
source: However, the key point is that properties of the polypeptides beyond their ability to oligomerize are clearly important determinants of cellular toxicity.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that non-toxic variants oligomerize but are not toxic.

claim: h-IAPP and Aβ40 have 25% amino acid identity.
source: h-IAPP and Aβ40 have 25% amino acid identity and 50% similarity
evidence: This is stated based on sequence comparison shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: h-IAPP and Aβ40 have 50% amino acid similarity.
source: h-IAPP and Aβ40 have 25% amino acid identity and 50% similarity
evidence: This is stated based on sequence comparison shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Aβ fibrils can seed amyloid formation by h-IAPP in vitro.
source: Aβ fibrils can seed amyloid formation by h-IAPP in vitro and in an animal model, and the two polypeptides interact in vitro (Andreetto et al., 2010; O'Nuallain et al., 2004; Oskarsson et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Andreetto et al., 2010; O'Nuallain et al., 2004; Oskarsson et al., 2015.

claim: Aβ fibrils can seed amyloid formation by h-IAPP in an animal model.
source: Aβ fibrils can seed amyloid formation by h-IAPP in vitro and in an animal model, and the two polypeptides interact in vitro (Andreetto et al., 2010; O'Nuallain et al., 2004; Oskarsson et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Andreetto et al., 2010; O'Nuallain et al., 2004; Oskarsson et al., 2015.

claim: h-IAPP and Aβ interact in vitro.
source: Aβ fibrils can seed amyloid formation by h-IAPP in vitro and in an animal model, and the two polypeptides interact in vitro (Andreetto et al., 2010; O'Nuallain et al., 2004; Oskarsson et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Andreetto et al., 2010; O'Nuallain et al., 2004; Oskarsson et al., 2015.

claim: Recent work has revealed significant levels of β-sheet structure in toxic oligomers from several proteins, including Aβ.
source: Recent work has revealed significant levels of β-sheet structure in toxic oligomers from several proteins, including Aβ (Chimon et al., 2007; Laganowsky et al., 2012; Lendel et al., 2014; Sandberg et al., 2010; Do et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated with multiple citations.

claim: Observation of partial helical structure in h-IAPP is consistent with studies of truncated h-IAPP analogs fused to maltose binding protein.
source: Observation of partial helical structure is consistent with studies of truncated h-IAPP analogs fused to maltose binding protein; as well as studies of h-IAPP aromatic residue mutants, and NMR studies of soluble IAPP variants (Wiltzius et al., 2009; Williamson et al., 2009; Tu and Raleigh, 2013).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Wiltzius et al., 2009; Williamson et al., 2009; Tu and Raleigh, 2013.

claim: Helical structure can be stabilized in h-IAPP by binding to negatively charged surfaces such as sulfated glycosaminoglycans.
source: It is also known that helical structure can be stabilized in h-IAPP by binding to negatively charged surfaces such as sulfated glycosaminoglycans or to vesicles containing significant amounts of anionic lipids (Wiltzius et al., 2009; Williamson et al., 2009; Tu and Raleigh, 2013; Brender et al., 2012; Knight et al., 2006; Meng et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated with multiple citations.

claim: Helical structure can be stabilized in h-IAPP by binding to vesicles containing significant amounts of anionic lipids.
source: It is also known that helical structure can be stabilized in h-IAPP by binding to negatively charged surfaces such as sulfated glycosaminoglycans or to vesicles containing significant amounts of anionic lipids (Wiltzius et al., 2009; Williamson et al., 2009; Tu and Raleigh, 2013; Brender et al., 2012; Knight et al., 2006; Meng et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated with multiple citations.

claim: 2D IR is a sensitive probe of β-sheet structure in aggregating systems.
source: 2D IR is a sensitive probe of β-sheet structure in aggregating systems (Buchanan et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2011; Strasfeld et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Buchanan et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2011; Strasfeld et al., 2009.

claim: The 2D IR spectrum of h-IAPP amyloid fibrils has significant intensity along the diagonal in the β-sheet region between 1615 and 1625 cm-1.
source: The spectrum of h-IAPP amyloid fibrils has significant intensity along the diagonal in the β-sheet region between 1615 and 1625 cm-1 (Figure 6A)
evidence: This is shown by 2D IR spectroscopy in Figure 6A.

claim: The 2D IR spectrum of h-IAPP lag phase intermediates is much less intense than the spectrum of amyloid fibrils.
source: The spectrum of the intermediates is much less intense than the spectrum of the amyloid fibrils, indicating only modest levels of β-sheet structure (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is shown by comparing 2D IR spectra in Figure 6A and B.

claim: Isotope edited 2D IR studies suggest that h-IAPP forms an intermediate with well developed, parallel, in-register β-structure in the FGAIL region during amyloid formation at high concentrations.
source: Recent isotope edited 2D IR studies using 10- to 20-fold higher h-IAPP concentrations than used herein (the isotope edited studies cannot currently be conducted at 40 µM peptide for technical reasons) suggest that h-IAPP forms an intermediate with well developed, parallel, in–register β-structure in the FGAIL region during amyloid formation under those conditions (Buchanan et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Buchanan et al., 2013.

claim: A β-sheet in the FGAIL region is fully consistent with the 2D IR data showing <15% overall β-sheet content.
source: A β-sheet of this size is fully consistent with the 2D IR data presented here.
evidence: This is stated as an inference reconciling different observations.

claim: ANS binds to toxic pre-amyloid oligomers formed by a range of amyloidogenic proteins.
source: ANS, a dye that is widely employed in protein folding studies to detect exposed hydrophobic patches and molten globule states (Figure 7A), binds to toxic pre-amyloid oligomers formed by a range of other amyloidogenic proteins, including various oligomers formed by the Aβ peptide, lysozyme, the α-synuclein protein of Parkinson's disease, SH3 domains, HypF-N, bovine serum albumin, concanavalin and others (Bolognesi et al., 2010; Mannini et al., 2014; Frare et al., 2009; Lorenzen et al., 2014; Bhattacharya et al., 2011; Fu et al., 2015; Ghosh et al., 2015; Paslawski et al., 2014; Vetri et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated with multiple citations.

claim: ANS binding is observed during the growth phase of h-IAPP amyloid formation.
source: No ANS binding is observed in the lag phase, but is observed during the growth phase of amyloid formation and in the saturation phase containing fibrils (Figure 7B and C).
evidence: This is shown by ANS fluorescence experiments in Figure 7B and C.

claim: ANS binding is observed in the saturation phase of h-IAPP amyloid formation containing fibrils.
source: No ANS binding is observed in the lag phase, but is observed during the growth phase of amyloid formation and in the saturation phase containing fibrils (Figure 7B and C).
evidence: This is shown by ANS fluorescence experiments in Figure 7B and C.

claim: bis-ANS binds to h-IAPP amyloid fibrils.
source: No binding to lag phase species is observed, but the dye, like ANS, binds to h-IAPP amyloid fibrils (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown by bis-ANS fluorescence experiments in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Nile Red does not bind to h-IAPP lag phase intermediates under the conditions of the study.
source: recent studies, conducted under different conditions than employed in our work, show that it does not bind to h-IAPP lag phase intermediates (Hawe et al., 2008; Jha et al., 2014; Krishnan et al., 2012; Sackett and Wolff, 1987). We independently confirmed that it does not bind to the lag phase species populated in our experiments (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown by Nile Red fluorescence experiments in Figure 7—figure supplement 1 and cited studies.

claim: The ensemble of toxic lag phase oligomers of h-IAPP are defined by being soluble, globally flexible, lacking extensive β-sheet structure, and not having persistent hydrophobic surface patches.
source: Collectively, the data show that the ensemble of toxic lag phase oligomers of h-IAPP are defined by the following characteristics: they are soluble, globally flexible, lack extensive β-sheet structure, and do not have persistent hydrophobic surface patches that allow ANS, bis-ANS or Nile Red binding.
evidence: This is a summary statement integrating multiple experimental findings.

claim: Toxic h-IAPP lag phase oligomers share similar features with those reported for a range of other amyloidogenic proteins, but are not identical to them.
source: This combination of properties indicates that toxic h-IAPP lag phase oligomers share similar features with those reported for a range of other amyloidogenic proteins, but are not identical to them (Bolognesi et al., 2010; Kim et al., 2009; Laganowsky et al., 2012; Mannini et al., 2014; Lendel et al., 2014; Sandberg et al., 2010; Frare et al., 2009; Lorenzen et al., 2014; Stroud et al., 2012; Chen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the data with citations to comparative studies.

claim: The distinct molecular features of toxic IAPP oligomers have important implications for rational design of drugs with improved specificity.
source: The distinct molecular features of toxic IAPP oligomers have important implications for rational design of drugs with improved specificity.
evidence: This is stated as an implication of the findings.

claim: Aromatic contacts (π-π interactions) have been proposed to play an important role in amyloid formation.
source: Aromatic contacts (π-π interactions) have been proposed to play an important role in amyloid formation.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Mutation of the three aromatic residues in h-IAPP to Leu slows the rate of amyloid formation.
source: Although they are not required for h-IAPP amyloid formation, mutation of the three aromatic residues in h-IAPP to Leu (3xL-IAPP) slows the rate of amyloid formation (Tu and Raleigh, 2013; Marek et al., 2007; Gazit, 2007).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Tu and Raleigh, 2013; Marek et al., 2007; Gazit, 2007.

claim: Aromatic residues are not an absolute requirement for h-IAPP amyloid formation.
source: Although they are not required for h-IAPP amyloid formation
evidence: This is stated and demonstrated by 3xL-IAPP forming amyloid (Figure 9).

claim: There are no persistent interactions between F15 and Y37 or F23 and Y37 in h-IAPP lag phase intermediates.
source: Our p-cyanoPhe experiments show that there are no persistent interactions between F15 and Y37 or F23 and Y37 of h-IAPP
evidence: This is inferred from p-cyanoPhe fluorescence data in Figure 8E.

claim: Aromatic residues contribute to h-IAPP toxicity.
source: indicating that aromatic residues, and hence π-π interactions, are not an absolute requirement for h-IAPP toxicity, but do contribute to it.
evidence: This is demonstrated by 3xL-IAPP being less toxic than h-IAPP (Figure 9F).

claim: An effective inhibitor of amyloid formation can be deleterious to cells if it does not prevent the formation or accumulation of toxic lag phase intermediates, but traps them instead in their toxic conformation.
source: We conclude that an effective inhibitor of amyloid formation can be deleterious to cells if it does not prevent the formation or the accumulation of toxic lag phase intermediates, but traps them instead in their toxic conformation.
evidence: This is concluded from experiments with I26P-IAPP as an inhibitor (Figure 10).

claim: Toxic h-IAPP species are partially structured, globally flexible, soluble, low order oligomers with solvated aromatic side chains that populate the lag phase of amyloid formation.
source: Toxic h-IAPP species are found to be partially structured, globally flexible, soluble, low order oligomers with solvated aromatic side chains that populate the lag phase of amyloid formation.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main findings.

claim: Studies with I26P-IAPP, TM-IAPP and r-IAPP demonstrate that not all IAPP oligomers are toxic.
source: Studies with I26P-IAPP, TM-IAPP and r-IAPP demonstrate that not all IAPP oligomers are toxic, decoupling general oligomerization from toxicity
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments showing these variants oligomerize but are not toxic (Figure 5).

claim: The conformational properties of IAPP oligomers and/or their stability, rather than their size, are important determinants of toxicity.
source: and suggest that the conformational properties of oligomers and/or their stability, rather than their size, are important determinants of toxicity.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that toxic and non-toxic oligomers have similar size distributions but different conformational properties.

claim: IM-MS studies indicated that low order r-IAPP and h-IAPP oligomers have different gas phase conformations.
source: Along these lines, IM-MS studies indicated that low order r-IAPP and h-IAPP oligomers have different gas phase conformations and exhibit different gas phase stabilities
evidence: This is stated with citation context to Young et al., 2014.

claim: IM-MS studies suggest that certain inhibitors of toxicity target subspecies of oligomers.
source: and suggest that certain inhibitors of toxicity target subspecies of oligomers (Young et al., 2014; Dupuis et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Young et al., 2014; Dupuis et al., 2009.

claim: Toxicity has been linked to the surface hydrophobicity of oligomers formed by other amyloidogenic proteins.
source: Toxicity has been linked to the surface hydrophobicity of oligomers formed by other amyloidogenic proteins (Mannini et al., 2014)
evidence: This is stated with citation to Mannini et al., 2014.

claim: Surface hydrophobicity does not rationalize the relative toxicity of the IAPP oligomers examined in this study.
source: but that does not appear to rationalize the relative toxicity of the oligomers examined here.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that h-IAPP oligomers do not bind ANS and the non-toxic variants have similar hydrophobicity.

claim: All of the non-toxic IAPP variants examined contain proline substitutions within a region of h-IAPP that has been postulated to form transient, parallel, in register β-sheet structure during amyloid formation.
source: but all of the non-toxic variants examined here contain proline substitutions within a region of h-IAPP that has been postulated to form transient, parallel, in register β-sheet structure during amyloid formation in solution.
evidence: This is stated based on sequence analysis and cited structural studies.

claim: The ability of proline to disrupt secondary structure in the FGAIL region may be an important feature in reducing toxicity.
source: The ability of proline to disrupt secondary structure in this region may well be an important feature in reducing toxicity.
evidence: This is speculated based on the observation that all non-toxic variants have proline substitutions.

claim: Toxic h-IAPP oligomers do not bind ANS, bis-ANS or Nile Red.
source: However, they do not bind ANS, bis-ANS or Nile Red
evidence: This is demonstrated by dye binding experiments in Figure 7 and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The overall β-sheet and α-helical content measured for the ensemble of toxic h-IAPP oligomers in solution is much less than that described for a range of other amyloidogenic proteins.
source: and the overall β-sheet and α-helical content measured for the ensemble of toxic h-IAPP oligomers in solution is much less than that described for a range of other amyloidogenic proteins.
evidence: This is stated based on CD and 2D IR data compared to literature reports.

claim: Isoforms of the Aβ peptide of AD have been shown to contain extensive regions of β-sheet structure.
source: Isoforms of the Aβ peptide of AD and a fragment derived from αB crystallin have been shown to contain extensive regions of β-sheet structure
evidence: This is stated with citation context.

claim: A fragment derived from αB crystallin has been shown to contain extensive regions of β-sheet structure.
source: Isoforms of the Aβ peptide of AD and a fragment derived from αB crystallin have been shown to contain extensive regions of β-sheet structure
evidence: This is stated with citation context.

claim: Oligomers formed from several other proteins are reported to be rich in α-helical structure.
source: while oligomers formed from several other proteins are reported to be rich in α-helical structure (Chiti and Dobson, 2006; Bolognesi et al., 2010; Chimon et al., 2007; Glabe, 2008; Kim et al., 2009; Laganowsky et al., 2012; Mannini et al., 2014; Lendel et al., 2014; Sandberg et al., 2010; Stroud et al., 2012; Chen et al., 2015; Sarkar et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated with multiple citations.

claim: The toxic h-IAPP intermediates differ from toxic oligomers described in other amyloidoses.
source: Thus, these data reveal, for the first time, that the toxic h-IAPP intermediates differ from toxic oligomers described in other amyloidoses (Campioni et al., 2010; Bolognesi et al., 2010; Chimon et al., 2007; Glabe, 2008; Kim et al., 2009; Laganowsky et al., 2012; Mannini et al., 2014; Lendel et al., 2014; Lorenzen et al., 2014; Sarkar et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as a key conclusion with citations to comparative studies.

claim: There is growing evidence that links type 2 diabetes and Alzheimer's disease.
source: given the growing evidence that links T2D and AD (Yang and Song, 2013; Oskarsson et al., 2015; Ninomiya, 2014).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Yang and Song, 2013; Oskarsson et al., 2015; Ninomiya, 2014.

claim: Pre-fibrillar forms of h-IAPP and Aβ interact in vitro.
source: Pre-fibrillar forms of h-IAPP and Aβ interact in vitro and a positive association has recently been demonstrated in plasma (Miklossy et al., 2010; Qiu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Miklossy et al., 2010; Qiu et al., 2014.

claim: A positive association between h-IAPP and Aβ has been demonstrated in plasma.
source: Pre-fibrillar forms of h-IAPP and Aβ interact in vitro and a positive association has recently been demonstrated in plasma (Miklossy et al., 2010; Qiu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Miklossy et al., 2010; Qiu et al., 2014.

claim: Aβ has been reported to form pancreatic deposits in type 2 diabetes.
source: Aβ has been reported to form pancreatic deposits in T2D, while h-IAPP has been reported in brain plaques in AD (O'Nuallain et al., 2004; Oskarsson et al., 2015; Miklossy et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated with citations to O'Nuallain et al., 2004; Oskarsson et al., 2015; Miklossy et al., 2010.

claim: h-IAPP has been reported in brain plaques in Alzheimer's disease.
source: Aβ has been reported to form pancreatic deposits in T2D, while h-IAPP has been reported in brain plaques in AD (O'Nuallain et al., 2004; Oskarsson et al., 2015; Miklossy et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated with citations to O'Nuallain et al., 2004; Oskarsson et al., 2015; Miklossy et al., 2010.

claim: Toxic species formed by different proteins can be distinct in their biophysical/biochemical properties, even when the two sequences share common features.
source: The data presented here demonstrate that toxic species formed by different proteins can be distinct in their biophysical/biochemical properties, even when the two sequences share common features
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from comparing h-IAPP and Aβ.

claim: Some inhibitors of h-IAPP amyloid formation do not inhibit Aβ amyloid formation and vice versa.
source: helping to rationalize why some inhibitors of h-IAPP amyloid formation do not inhibit Aβ amyloid formation and vice versa (Rochet, 2007; Wang and Raleigh, 2014).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Rochet, 2007; Wang and Raleigh, 2014.

claim: Therapeutic strategies for amyloidosis diseases need to be tailored to the specific molecular properties of pathological amyloidogenic species unique to each disease.
source: This is important since it indicates that therapeutic strategies for amyloidosis diseases need to be tailored to the specific molecular properties of pathological amyloidogenic species unique to each disease.
evidence: This is stated as an implication of the findings.

claim: Inhibitors that stabilize the ensemble of toxic lag phase intermediates can trap them and exacerbate pathological cellular cascades.
source: Inhibitors that stabilize the ensemble of toxic lag phase intermediates can trap them and exacerbate pathological cellular cascades.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments with I26P-IAPP (Figure 10).

claim: Toxicity appears to be conformation dependent.
source: This observation provides additional evidence that toxicity appears to be conformation dependent
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that inhibitors can prolong toxicity by stabilizing toxic conformations.

claim: Caution must be taken when in vitro biophysical assays are used to develop leads for anti-amyloid agents.
source: The findings also emphasize that caution must be taken when in vitro biophysical assays are used, such as thioflavin-T binding, to develop leads for anti-amyloid agents
evidence: This is stated as an implication of the findings about inhibitors.

claim: Drugs that slow the onset of amyloid formation and cause the buildup of toxic pre-fibrillar intermediates can give the same spectroscopic signatures as compounds that slow amyloid formation but decrease the steady state population of toxic species.
source: since drugs that slow the onset of amyloid formation and cause the buildup of toxic pre-fibrillar intermediates can give the same spectroscopic signatures as compounds that slow amyloid formation, but decrease the steady state population of toxic species.
evidence: This is stated as a cautionary note about interpreting inhibitor screening assays.

claim: Compounds that accelerate amyloid formation could reduce toxicity by reducing the transient population of toxic oligomers.
source: Conversely, compounds that accelerate amyloid formation could reduce toxicity by reducing the transient population of toxic oligomers (Bieschke et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Bieschke et al., 2012.

claim: Amyloid formation by different proteins may share many common features, but toxic species produced by different proteins can have different properties.
source: This work illustrates the power of combining time-resolved kinetic studies with physio-chemical, biochemical and biological measurements, and highlights that while amyloid formation by different proteins may share many common features, toxic species produced by different proteins can have different properties.
evidence: This is stated as a key conclusion of the work.

claim: Flexible, low order, toxic h-IAPP oligomers with modest overall β-sheet and α-helical content, which form before amyloid fibrils, are primary targets for therapeutic interventions.
source: In the case of pancreatic islet amyloidosis, we conclude that flexible, low order, toxic h-IAPP oligomers with modest overall β-sheet and α-helical content, which form before amyloid fibrils, are primary targets for therapeutic interventions.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion for therapeutic targeting.

claim: Molecules that decrease the population of toxic amyloidogenic species by preventing their formation, reducing their lifetime, or sequestering them may serve as therapeutic agents in disorders characterized by pancreatic β-cell dysfunction.
source: Hence, molecules that decrease the population of toxic amyloidogenic species by preventing their formation, reducing their lifetime, or sequestering them to prevent their interactions with cells may serve as therapeutic agents in disorders characterized by pancreatic β-cell dysfunction, and more broadly to a wide range of other protein misfolding diseases (Westermark et al., 2011; Campioni et al., 2010; Johnson et al., 2012; Blancas-Mejía and Ramirez-Alvarado, 2013).
evidence: This is stated as a therapeutic implication with citations.
